Bench-Scale Liquid-Phase Microaeration and Iron Dosing
Comparison for In Situ Biogas Desulfurization and Antibiotic
Resistance Management in Mesophilic Anaerobic Digestion
Seyed Mohammad Mirsoleimani Azizi, Basem S. Zakaria, Nervana Haffiez, Parisa Niknejad,

ABSTRACT: Microaeration and iron dosing are promising in situ
desulfurization methods for anaerobic digestion (AD). However, limited
reports exist on their systematic comparison. Consequently, this study
investigated liquid-phase microaeration (60−106 mL air/Lreactor/d) and
ferric chloride (250−650 mg FeCl3/L) dosages in mesophilic AD of
sewage sludge operated at a solid residence time of 20 days. Both
methods provided up to 88% H2S removal and moderate siloxane
removal (30−37%) but had no apparent impact on mercaptan removal
from biogas. However, the control and test reactors demonstrated
equivalent AD performance in terms of biomethane yields, chemical
oxygen demand, and total/volatile solids degradation efficiencies,
indicating that air and iron dosages were primarily utilized for biogas
desulfurization. Still, both methods resulted in substantial changes in
microbial community composition. Notably, the indication of syntrophy between facultative microbes and hydrogenotrophic
methanogens was intensified by both methods. For both methods, antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) and mobile genetic element
(MGE) abundances in digestate decreased considerably due to the decrease in the abundance of potential ARG hosts. Compared to
iron dosing, MGE removal was slightly higher in the microaeration reactor. These findings provide valuable insights into the efficacy
of these two approaches in desulfurization and the reduction of antibiotic resistance in AD.
KEYWORDS: anaerobic digestion, sludge, in situ biogas desulfurization, siloxanes, mercaptans, microaeration, iron dosing,
antibiotic resistance genes
■INTRODUCTION
In most centralized water resource recovery facilities (WRRFs)
worldwide, mesophilic or thermophilic anaerobic digestion
(AD) is widely practiced for sludge stabilization.1,2 Biogas from
AD can be used to co-generate heat and electricity or can be
upgraded to renewable natural gas (RNG). However, extensive
purification requirements of biogas to remove hydrogen sulfide
(H2S), mercaptans, and volatile organic compounds (e.g.,
siloxanes) limit its conversion to heat/electricity/RNG,
resulting in ubiquitous biogas flaring instead.3 Particularly,
excessive H2S and mercaptans in the biogas can cause
corrosion of metal pipes, combustion engines, and biogas
utilization equipment.3 Moreover, silicon dioxide particles
produced from the combustion of siloxanes can cause extensive
damage to process equipment by erosion or blockage.4 The
release of sulfur oxides (SOx) in flue gases is increasingly
becoming subject to air quality monitoring and permit
restrictions. Thus, regardless of biogas end use, reducing
sulfides allows WRRFs to maintain high operational and safety
standards and better odor control.
Established biogas desulfurization methods include various
end-of-the-pipe, ex situ approaches, such as scrubbing, biofilter,
biotrickling filters, absorption, and adsorption, where the
biogas is cleaned ex situ in a separate downstream treatment
unit.5 Despite being commercially available and implemented
to full-scale, ex situ methods (e.g., absorption) are usually
considered expensive (US $0.244−2.38/m3 biogas).5 Thus,
researchers have explored the use of in situ approaches, such as
microaeration and iron salt addition, for biogas desulfurization.
Microaeration is operated via controlled injection of a small
amount of air or pure oxygen into the headspace or liquid
phase of digesters.6 At low oxygen levels, sulfide can be
biochemically oxidized to elemental sulfur and/or sulfate. Iron

(salts/oxides) dosing is another approach to achieving in situ
desulfurization.5 Liquid-phase microaeraion can be operated
through various methods, such as injecting directly into the
digester, in the sludge feeding process, or through a
recirculation line. Liquid-phase microaeration is often recom-
mended for its ease of operation and control and has been
shown to be effective in full-scale applications.5 Divalent (Fe2+)
and trivalent (Fe3+) iron salts are commonly used and can
react with sulfide to form iron sulfide precipitates.5,6 As
summarized in a recent review report,6 a few full-scale
demonstrations have already been reported for both methods,
showing effective H2S removal (72−99%) performance.
Although most studies focused on mesophilic AD, studies
suggested that both methods could be effective for mesophilic
and thermophilic AD. Compared to ex situ desulfurization
technologies, microaeration and iron dosing have emerged as
potential low-cost alternatives (∼US $0.01−0.016/m3 bio-
gas).5 These methods are mostly localized within the digester
and limit dissolved sulfide conversion to H2S.5 However,
microaeration is considered relatively underdeveloped due to
its commercial unavailability, lack of estimated costs associated
with the maintenance of digesters in case of elemental sulfur
deposition, and safety concerns around dosing the incorrect
amount of oxygen/air.6 Although both methods have been
widely explored as low-cost alternatives for biogas desulfuriza-
tion, there is limited information on their systematic
comparison for biogas desulfurization and efficacy in removing
other contaminants such as mercaptans and siloxanes from
biogas.
Iron dosing for desulfurization is often considered as a
relatively more established method than microaeration, as it
has been widely used for sulfide removal in sewer systems for
many years.7 However, the use of microaeration for in situ
biogas desulfurization has recently received attention as it is
considered the chemical-free treatment alternative, potentially
resulting in less cost.5,6 Nonetheless, a recent economic
analysis report based on data collected from different studies
suggested that the operating costs of the two methods would
be competitive, e.g., US $0.01/m3 for iron dosing versus US
$0.016/m3 for microaeration.5 The water sector would benefit
from further systematic comparisons using performance data
collected under identical test conditions to provide a more
reliable decision support tool in process selection.
Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are considered as
hotspots for antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) propagation and
transmission to other ecosystems.8 High concentrations of
residual antibiotics and pathogenic microorganisms in WWTPs
are stimulating the resistance prevalence among microbial
communities.8,9 ARGs can be disseminated among microbial
communities by horizontal gene transfer (HGT) via mobile
genetic elements (MGEs) such as plasmids and integrons (i.e.,
intl1 and intl2) that are considered as biomarkers for HGT.10,11
A few recent reports also suggested that both methods
(microaeration and iron dosing) could improve the removal of
ARGs and MGEs in AD and limit their transmission to our
ecosystem to a certain extent.12,13 The deaths related to
antibiotic-resistant infections have rapidly increased globally in
recent years, raising concerns regarding potential ARG/MGE
spread routes.14 As the land application of digestate presents a
major route of ARG/MGE spread,15 enhancing their removal
along with desulfurization would be an added benefit and a
step toward achieving the circular economy and environmental
sustainability. As of now, no study on a systematic comparison
of the effectiveness of these two methods in removing ARGs/
MGEs has been reported in the literature.
To fill the aforementioned research gaps, this study presents
a systematic, bench-scale comparison of liquid-phase microa-
eration and iron dosing for in situ biogas desulfurization in
mesophilic AD of sewage sludge. First, the effects of two
methods on H2S, mercaptan, and siloxane removals were
investigated along with AD performance. Moreover, variations
of ARG/MGE abundances and microbial communities were
analyzed. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, in the past, no
such comprehensive report was available for the comparison of
these two methods under identical experimental conditions.
■MATERIALS AND METHODS
Experimental Set-Up. The experiments were carried out
using six identical glass anaerobic bioreactors (ISES-Canada,
Vaughan, ON, Canada) with working and total volumes of 1.5
and 2 L, respectively. The bioreactors are equipped with
mechanical agitators coupled with electrical motors and reactor
lids with ports that can be used for either gas collection or
injection (Figure S1). Bioreactors were operated in a water
bath (VWR Water bath 28L, 120V, VWR Canada, Mississauga,
ON, Canada) to maintain a mesophilic operating condition at
37 ± 1 °C. The liquids were stirred with agitators at 200 rpm.
Duplicate bioreactors were operated for each condition, and
average results are reported here.
Sludge Characteristics. The digested sludge (inoculum)
and AD feed sludge used for the experiments were collected
from a wastewater treatment plant in Edmonton (Alberta,
Canada). The digested sludge was collected once during the
start-up of the reactors, while the AD feedstock sludge was
collected monthly. Before use, all samples were stored at 4 °C
in a cold room, for a period of 1−4 weeks, depending on the
sampling frequency. Before the start-up of the reactors, the
inoculum was pre-incubated for a few days at 37 °C for
acclimation of microbial communities and residual organics
degradation. The average characteristics of digested sludge
were as follows: total chemical oxygen demand (TCOD): 23 ±
0.1 g/L, soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD): 3.5 ± 0.1
g/L, total solids (TS): 29 ± 1 g/L, volatile solids (VS): 24 ± 2
g/L, alkalinity: 9.5 ± 0.6 g/L as CaCO3, and pH: 7.1 ± 0.1.
The average feed sludge characteristics were as follows:
TCOD: 70 ± 4 g/L, SCOD: 7.1 ± 0.4 g/L, TS: 43 ± 2 g/
L, VS: 36 ± 2 g/L, dissolved sulfide (S2−): 35 ± 1 mg/L, and
pH: 6.9 ± 0.2.
Start-Up, Operation, and Experimental Phases.
During start-up, 750 mL of inoculum and 750 mL of AD
feed sludge (substrate) were added to each digester. Thus, the
initial ratio of feed to inoculum was set at 1.5 (VS basis),
following recommended ratios of ≤2 found in the
literature,16,17 to prevent excessive organic loading in the
digesters. The bioreactors were purged with nitrogen gas for 5
min to ensure anaerobic conditions. For the first 3 days,
reactors were operated in a batch mode, and then the
operation was switched to a semicontinuous mode. A solid
residence time (SRT) of 20 days was selected for the
experiment to mimic AD conditions at the wastewater
treatment plant. Based on the working volume of the reactor,
the sludge was fed to the bioreactor at a rate of 75 mL/d using
peristaltic pumps (Longer Pump BT100−2 J, Langer Instru-
ments Corp, Tucson, AZ), which corresponds to the organic
loading rate (OLR) of 1.47 kg COD/m3/d. Before starting
experiments with microaeration and iron dosing, all six reactors

was referred to as the ‘pre-experimental phase’. It should be
noted that SRT (20 days) remained constant throughout the
operation of 125 days. Based on the observed methane yields
and the removal of organics (discussed later), it was evident
that the dosages of iron and microaeration employed during
the entire operation remained low, thereby having minimal
impact on methane productivity and kinetics. The primary
objective of the pre-experimental phase was to establish that
biogas yield and quality were consistent across all reactors, thus
providing a baseline for commencing microaeration and iron
dosing experiments. This approach enables a reliable
comparison of different conditions (i.e., control vs microaera-
tion vs iron dosing) regarding their effects on AD performance.
After ensuring comparable performance (based on methane
gas production and H2S content) from all six reactors,
microaeration and iron dosing experiments were started in
duplicate. Four reactors were used for microaeration and iron
dosing experiments, and two reactors were operated as a
control (without microaeration or iron dosing). For microa-
eration operation, the air was injected directly into the liquid
phase through the gas injection port located in the lids of the
reactors using a peristaltic pump. However, the pump was
intermittently operated every 4 h for a specific time to maintain
the target daily air supply rate (Table 1). The total pump run
time for the microaeration operation in phase-1, phase-2, and
phase-3 were 5, 10, and 15 min per day, respectively. The
selected microaeration conditions (40−106 mL air/Lreactor/d)
were within the range of effective microaeration conditions,
providing >80% H2S removal, reported in the literature (3−
160 mL air/Lreactor/d).18−21 It should be noted that some
studies also used extremely high microaeration with air, which
could cause the dilution of biogas. For instance, Yang and
Deng22 studied microaeration by injecting air at 66.7 mL/L/
min in a 4.5 L digester (i.e., 21,344 mL air/Lreactor/d). Among
different forms of iron (di- and trivalent salts/oxides) used for
in situ desulfurization, Fe (III) is known to provide faster
reaction kinetics and is also effective for a wide pH range.23,24
Therefore, ferric chloride (FeCl3) was selected for this testing.
For iron dosing, feed sludge was amended with FeCl3
(iron(III) chloride, reagent grade, 97%, Sigma Aldrich,
Canada) before daily feeding. As summarized in Table 1,
three different dosages of microaeration and FeCl3 have been
tested in this study.
Analytical Methods. TCOD, SCOD, and alkalinity were
measured using the HACH reagent kits (HACH Co.,
Loveland, CO). For SCOD analysis, samples were filtered
using 0.45 μm membrane filters. For COD analysis, HACH
COD standard solution (1000 mg/L as COD) and deionized
water were used as the standard and blank, respectively. The
total solid (TS) and volatile solid (VS) concentrations were
measured using standard methods (2540 Solids).25 pH was
measured using a bench-top pH meter (Accumet AR15, Fisher
Scientific, Pittsburgh, PA). The oxygen reduction potential
(ORP) was measured with a portable ORP meter (Milwaukee
MW500, ORP Meter with platinum electrode, ±1000 mV, 1
mV resolution, ±5 mV accuracy, Milwaukee Instruments,
Rocky Mount, NC). Dissolved sulfide (S2−) was measured
using the Hach Sulfide Reagent Set, methylene blue
(#2244500, Hach Canada, London, ON). To avoid high
sulfide concentrations which can inhibit the full-color develop-
ment, samples were diluted (10 times).
Biogas produced from the bioreactors was collected in gas
bags, and then volumes were measured using frictionless glass
syringes. Biogas composition (CH4, H2, and CO2 content) was
analyzed using gas chromatography (7890B, Agilent Tech-
nologies, Santa Clara) equipped with a thermal conductivity
detector (TCD) and two columns (Molsieve 5A 60/80 mesh
and Hayesep N 80−100 mesh). All methane production data
were expressed at standard temperature and pressure (STP) (0
°C, 1 atm). Gaseous H2S concentrations were measured with a
portable H2S gas monitor (Acrulog H2S Short Deployment
Gas Monitor 0−2000 ppm, Model ACRSD2000, Detection
Instruments Corp., Phoenix, AZ). After each measurement, the
sampling tubes were purged with clean air before the following
measurement. Siloxane and mercaptan concentrations in
biogas were analyzed by ALS Environmental (Waterloo, ON,
Canada). Siloxane analysis was performed using procedures
adapted from EPA Method TO-17, ISO Method 16017, and
NIOSH Method 2549. Collected biogas samples actively
collected on thermal desorption sorbent tubes were thermally
stripped, and the analytes were recollected on the trapping
material of a focusing trap in the thermal desorber. The
analytes were then thermally desorbed into a thermal
desorption−gas chromatography−mass spectrometry (TD-
GC-MS) system for analysis. Mercaptan concentrations were
analyzed by gas chromatography with a sulfur chemilumines-
cent detector (SCD). The analysis was performed using
procedures adapted from ASTM D5504. Biogas samples are
collected into cleaned evacuated silica-coated canisters. By
means of a loop system, a volume of biogas is transferred from
the canister and cryofocused before determining the mercaptan
compounds by GC-SCD.
Microbial Community and DNA Extraction. After the
completion of phase-3, digested sludge samples were
aseptically collected from each treatment for the bacterial
and archaeal community analysis. After centrifugation at 15
min at 2000×g, the pellet (0.25 g) was taken for the genomic
DNA extraction using the PowerSoil DNA Isolation Kit
(MoBio Laboratories, Carlsbad) as per the manufacturer’s
instructions. The quality and yield of the extracted DNA were
detected by a spectrophotometer (NanoDrop 2000C, Thermo
Scientific). The genomic DNA was sent to the Research and
Testing Laboratory (Lubbock, TX) for Illumina Miseq
sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene using the universal primer
set 515F/806R.10 For the microbial community and diversity,
the raw sequencing data were processed using the Quantitative
Insights Into Microbial Ecology (QIIME) pipeline (QIIME2,
Version 2021.2). The detailed methodology can be found

Quantification of ARGs. Tetracycline resistance genes
(tetM, tetQ, tetX, tetW, tetB, and tetA), sulfonamide resistance
genes (sul1 and sul2), β-lactam resistance genes (blaTEM), and
macrolide resistance genes (ermC and ermB) were evaluated by
the quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR). Similarly,
MGEs including integrons (intl1 and intl2) were quantified by
qPCR. The detailed quantification procedures were performed
according to the QuantiFast SYBR Green PCR Kit’s protocol
using the CFX 96 real-time PCR system with a C1000
Thermal Cycler (Bio-Rad). The detailed methodology and
primers can be found elsewhere.8
Data Analysis. Student’s t-test was conducted using
Microsoft Excel to identify statistically significant differences
in the results based on average values at a 95% confidence
level. To analyze the relationship between ARG gene copies
and the relative abundance of the microbial community,
correlation analysis was conducted using Spearman’s Rho
coefficient. The correlation was visualized using a correlation
plot, which was created using the R software (RStudio v.
1.4.1103). The correlation was represented by a range of values
from −1 to +1 and p-values less than 0.05 were considered to
be statistically significant.
■RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Anaerobic Digestion Performance. Figure 1 shows the
daily methane production from bioreactors under different
operating conditions over 125 days of operation. Between days
1−34, all reactors were operated under identical conditions,
i.e., the pre-experimental phase without microaeration and iron
dosing, to establish a baseline for subsequent comparison.
During the first week of operation, methane production
profiles in all reactors showed considerable fluctuations.
However, the daily methane production rate slightly decreased
and stabilized during the following week. This stable daily
methane production continued slightly over a week. After day
17, the daily methane production slightly increased in all
reactors. However, between days 20−34, average daily
methane production in control, microaeration, and iron-
dosed reactors were comparable (0.22 ± 0.05, 0.19 ± 0.08,
0.21 ± 0.06 L CH4/Lreactor/d, respectively). Furthermore,
methane content (vol.%) in biogas produced from these
reactors was quite similar (50 ± 2, 51 ± 5, and 52 ± 5%,
respectively) (p-value = 0.235) (see Figure S2). The H2S
content in biogas measured between days 25−28 was also
comparable (p-value = 0.606) in all reactors (see Figure S2).
Thus, despite some fluctuations, all reactors showed quite
similar performance in terms of methane productivity and
biogas quality (i.e., CH4 and H2S content). Therefore, this
state was considered a baseline for starting microaeration and
iron dosing experiments, allowing a reliable comparison among
different conditions (i.e., control vs microaeration vs iron
dosing).
On day 35, phase-1 operation of microaeration (40 mL air/
Lreactor/d) and iron (250 mg FeCl3/L) dosing was started and
was continued until day 46 (Figure 1). During that period,
methane production and methane content in biogas increased
in all reactors and reached a pseudo-steady-state. The average
daily methane production in the control, microaeration, and
iron-dosed reactors were 0.39 ± 0.05, 0.41 ± 0.02, and 0.44 ±
0.06 L CH4/Lreactor/d, respectively. The methane contents
(Figure 1b) in biogas were 56 ± 2% (control), 57 ± 3%
(microaeration), and 59 ± 3% (iron dosing). Thus, methane
production and methane content in biogas were similar for all
conditions. As discussed later, only H2S content in biogas was
appreciably impacted by microaeration and iron dosing. Thus,
air and iron dosages selected for phase-1 were mostly utilized
for desulfurization without impacting the methanogenic
activity. If these technologies were to affect methanogenic
activity adversely, they would not be appealing to the
management of AD facilities.
Consequently, to examine the impact of increased
microaeration and iron dosing, air and iron dosages were
increased during phases 2 and 3. Compared to phase-1, air and
iron dosages were doubled during phase-2 (days 47−94).
However, analogous to phase-1, the methane production rate
and methane content remained unaffected (Figure 1). Daily
methane production in the control, microaeration, and iron-
dosed reactors were 0.40 ± 0.02, 0.42 ± 0.02, and 0.42 ± 0.02
L CH4/Lreactor/d, respectively. The methane contents in biogas
were 55 ± 1, 57 ± 2, and 57 ± 1%, respectively (Figure 1).
Thus, daily methane production and methane content in
biogas were comparable between the two phases (phase-1 and
-2) despite significant differences in air (40 vs 80 mL air/
Lreactor/d) and iron (250 vs 500 mg FeCl3/L) dosages. Despite

Figure S3 illustrates effluent TCOD, SCOD, TS, and VS
concentrations under different operating conditions. Under
each phase, effluent TCOD, SCOD, TS, and VS concen-
trations were comparable in all reactors. Thus, these data also
corroborate the methane production profiles. Considering the
theoretical methane yield of 350 mL CH4/g CODremoved at
STP, the COD mass balances computed based on
experimental methane production and TCOD removal
indicated a closure of 90 to 120% (see Figure S3), thus
emphasizing data reliability.28
As discussed later, H2S content in biogas in microaeration
and iron-dosed reactors gradually decreased between phase-1
and phase-3 (discussed later). Thus, microaeration and iron
dosing appeared to have a trivial impact on methane
production and were primarily utilized for biogas desulfuriza-
tion. To date, a few studies investigated liquid-phase
microaeration.18,21,22,29 Jeníček et al.21 and Yang and Deng22
reported that microaeration could increase methane produc-
tion by 17% and 6.4−19.6%, respectively. Notably, Yang and
Deng22 suggested that methane production increased due to
enhanced hydrolysis triggered by microaeration. However, the
authors used considerably higher air dosing (66.7 mL/L/min
in a 4.5 L digester) than our study, while H2S in biogas was
lower than in our reactors (336 ppm vs ∼550−900 ppm). It is
expected that the differences in feedstock type, OLRs, SRTs,
microaeration dosages, and sulfide levels may lead to different
results. For instance, Nghiem et al.29 reported no impact on
methane production due to microaeration. Two previous
reports based on full-scale demonstrations of iron (ferrous and
ferric) also suggested a minimal effect on methane production
while considerably reducing H2S content in biogas.30 Thus, the
trivial impact of microaeration and FeCl3 on methane
production observed in our study was consistent with the
literature.
A few reports previously raised concerns that microaeration
with air instead of pure oxygen would cause the dilution of
biogas with nitrogen gas,31,32 which would reduce methane
content. Although we did not measure nitrogen content in
biogas, the average biogas methane content from the
microaeration reactor was slightly higher than the control
during all experimental phases (see Figure 1b). Thus, there was
no sign of decreased methane content in biogas. Jeníček et al.21
also previously demonstrated that microaeration with air would
not considerably reduce methane content in biogas in full-scale
anaerobic digesters; the maximum decrease in methane
concentration was <2%. Interestingly, using pure oxygen
instead of air has often been recommended by previous
studies (mostly related to gas-phase microaeration) to avoid
the dilution of biogas.32 However, our results further suggested
no requirement of replacing air with pure oxygen during liquid-
phase microaeration, which can often be expensive.21 It should
be noted that combining oxygen with biogas is typically viewed
unfavorably due to the risk of explosions linked to methane/
oxygen mixtures. Despite the amount of pure oxygen dosed for
microaeration being very small and may be quickly consumed,
it is crucial to acknowledge that the risk of explosion is always
present when working with pure oxygen for microaeration in
AD, and should not be underestimated, as suggested in the
literature.6,32 Therefore, from an operational standpoint, AD
facilities generally prefer not to work with pure oxygen for
safety reasons, if possible. This makes air injection a more
practical and cost-effective solution.
H2S Removal from Biogas. Figure 2a shows H2S content
in biogas during different experimental phases. During the pre-
experimental phase, baseline H2S content in the control,
microaeration, and FeCl3 reactor were 956 ± 173, 849 ± 51,
and 879 ± 271 ppm, respectively. In phase-1, H2S content in
the control, microaeration, and FeCl3 reactors were 555 ± 66,
407 ± 44, and 308 ± 70 ppm, respectively (Figure 2a).

in the control digester considerably decreased (p-value =

content in biogas was measured between days 25−28. The
reactors did not reach a steady state at that time. Furthermore,

The maximum H2S removal efficiencies observed for liquid-
phase microaeration and FeCl3 dosing (up to 88%) was within
the range of high H2S removal efficiencies previously reported
in the literature (liquid-phase microaeration: 70−99%; FeCl3
dosing: 72−99%).6,23 However, in phase-1, microaeration
provided considerably lower desulfurization efficiencies than
FeCl3 (27 vs 45%). The process of microaeration integrates
both chemical and biological reactions for H2S removal.5,33
Particularly, the enrichment of sulfide-oxidizing bacteria
(SOB) was reported as the key factor in microaerobic
desulfurization.32 It is expected that enriching the sulfide-
oxidizing bacterial community would require some time. For
instance, a previous study suggested that a full-scale micro-
aerobic anaerobic digester would require 3−12 weeks to reach
a stable desulfurization performance.21 Jensen et al.34 reported
SOB median growth rates of 1.25 and 1.33 d−1 as determined
from the utilization rates of hydrogen sulfide and oxygen. Iron
salts (e.g., FeCl3) can react with dissolved sulfide to form
insoluble iron sulfide via chemical precipitation, consequently
preventing the stripping of H2S into the biogas.5 Based on a
full-scale demonstration, Erdirencelebi and Kucukhemek30
reported that the digesters stabilized within 11 days after the
FeCl3 was started. Thus, it can be assumed that the response of
the digester to iron dosing would be relatively faster than
microaeration. Nonetheless, during phase-2, microaeration
could provide slightly higher average H2S removal than
FeCl3 (76 vs 80%), and comparable performance in phase-3.
Analogous to H2S levels in biogas, dissolved sulfide (S2−)
concentrations were comparable in microaeration (9.5 ± 1
mg/L) and iron-dosed (9.7 ± 1 mg/L) reactors in phase-3
(see Figure 2b). In contrast, dissolved sulfide concentration in
the control was relatively higher (18 ± 1 mg/L). Considering
the initial dissolved sulfide level of 35 ± 1 mg/L, dissolved
sulfide removal efficiencies (72−73%) were lower than H2S
removal efficiencies in biogas. Previously, Krayzelova et al.35
reported that dissolved sulfide removal was only 20−30%,
while H2S removal in biogas was as high as 79% with liquid-
phase microaeration. Such an observation can be explained by
the fact that H2S oxidation also takes place in the headspace,
even when air is injected into the liquid phase.35 Furthermore,
the degradation of sulfur-containing proteins (mostly sludge-
bound proteins) can also produce additional sulfides and
mercaptans. It should be noted that concentrations of
dissolved sulfide and H2S in the digester may change with

not shown). Digester pH remained almost stable (at ∼7.5)
throughout the operating period in all reactors. Thus, it was
confirmed that the differences in biogas H2S levels were not
attributed to any pH changes.

reactor had a slightly higher total abundance of integrons (int1
and int2). A few studies previously suggested that microaera-

ARGs/MGE hosts, genera Pseudomonas and Solibacillus48,49
were the most abundant in the control reactor (discussed

To further investigate the relationship between ARG
abundance and microbial communities, a correlation analysis
was conducted (Figure 6). A strong positive correlation was
observed between the high abundance of ARG copies and the
enrichment of Solibacillus (r = 0.98) and Pseudomonas (r = 1).
On the other hand, all other genera showed a high negative
correlation with the total ARG gene copies. For instance,
Aminobacterium (r = −0.99), Caldicoprobacter (r = −97),
Cloacamonaceae_W22 (r = −0.94), Clostridium (r = −0.76),
and Anaerolinaceae__T78 (r = −0.7) showed a relatively weak
correlation with ARG copies. Thus, the results indicated that
potential changes in microbial communities due to microaera-
tion and iron dosing could be the critical factor influencing the
proliferation of ARGs/MGEs. However, caution should be
exercised when interpreting such correlations, as the
composition of bacterial communities often follows seasonal
patterns.58 Although the composition of ARGs does not
typically show such seasonality, the absolute abundance of
ARGs in incoming sludge may vary between winter and
summer months.59 Thus, the temporal patterns of microbial
taxonomy and function may be asynchronous or uncoupled
and warrant further investigation.
Significance of Results and Future Considerations.
The results suggested that both methods could be effective for
H2S removal (up to 88%) from biogas. Both methods could
provide additional benefits in terms of higher ARG/MGE
removal than the control. However, depending on the end use
of biogas, downstream purification processes may still be
required to remove mercaptans, residual siloxane, and H2S. For
instance, siloxane concentrations below 0.03−30 mg/m3 have
been recommended for biogas utilization in combined heat
and power (CHP) plants.60,61 Overall, considering the
technical performance observed in this study, there was no
clear winner between the two methods. In addition to capital
costs, the differences in electricity cost for microaeration
operation and chemical cost may considerably impact process
economics. Electricity prices may fluctuate considerably, and
the costs of chemicals are subject to supply chain interruptions,
as noticed in recent years. The iron dosing would also require
the operation of a chemical dosing pump and paddle mixer,
increasing the operating costs via electricity usage. Also,
maintaining a continuous supply of chemicals (iron salt) can
often be a concern for some facilities. Therefore, detailed
capital costs and maintenance requirements/costs should be
assessed along with the technical performance.
■CONCLUSIONS
This study compared microaeration and iron dosing for in situ
biogas desulfurization in AD. Up to 88% H2S removal
efficiencies were achieved with both methods. Moderate
siloxane D4 removals (30−37%) were achieved with both
methods, but they appeared to be ineffective for mercaptan
removal. Despite no impact on methane production and sludge
degradation efficiencies, both methods could alter microbial
community composition by increasing the abundance of
certain fermentative and facultative microbes and hydro-
genotrophic methanogens compared with the control. The
removal of most ARGs/MGEs was also enhanced in test
reactors, which also corroborated with a decrease in potential
ARG/MGE hosts. However, the transferability of these results
to a full-scale application would require further site-specific
assessment, pilot refinement, and economic evaluations.
Furthermore, future research should prioritize long-term
operations and delve into process design, control/monitoring,
and maintenance requirements of these methods.
